documents.title: Guidelines for Using Generative Artificial Intelligence in Instructional Settings at UCR
documents.summary: Provost guidelines set six principles for generative AI in instruction (beneficial use, equity, information security, local authority, accountability, transparency) and suggest practices for instructors. The Instructor of Record decides whether and how students may use AI, within data-security rules.
documents.stance_why: The document sets no university rule on student AI use. Principle 4 says "the Instructor of Record has broad latitude to determine whether and how generative AI may be used", and the practices only suggest what instructors "consider", so the decision is delegated. Coder B reached the same stance.

units.why: The preamble says "UCR is committed to equipping our students, faculty, and staff with the knowledge and skills to appropriately and effectively utilize generative AI", a statement that effective AI use is a skill the university wants to build, so P44; it informs for everyone.
units.anchor: committed to equipping our students, faculty, and staff with the knowledge and skills
units.resolution_why: The sentence is the university's own commitment ('UCR is committed to equipping'), so it is addressed as an institutional commitment, admin; A coded all.
units.fit_note: Framed as an institutional commitment to equip all members, not only a course-level professional-skill claim; also resembles training provision (P70).

units.why: The guidelines call themselves "a foundational resource for responsibly integrating these powerful tools into instructional settings", an institution-level statement of purpose and scope, so P56.
units.anchor: foundational resource for responsibly integrating these powerful tools into instructional settings
units.resolution_why: A coded admin, B all. The sentence describes the guidelines document itself as an institutional resource, so admin.

units.why: Principle 1 says use "by instructors or students, should aim to improve the learning experience for students"; it is an institution-wide principle for any AI use, so P56, with should modality.
units.anchor: should aim to improve the learning experience for students and better position students
units.resolution_why: A coded P56, B P83. P83 requires AI decisions to follow stated learning objectives; Principle 1 names none and only says any use 'should aim to improve the learning experience'. It is a general principle in the framework, so P56.
units.fit_note: Asks that AI use improve learning and future success generally; does not mention course or program learning objectives.

units.why: Principle 2 says "Students must have equal access to generative AI tools when used in instructional settings", an equity-of-access rule, so P51.
units.anchor: Students must have equal access to generative AI tools when used in instructional settings
units.resolution_why: A coded instructor/during-work, B all/general. 'Students must have equal access ... when used in instructional settings' is a principle binding whoever deploys AI in instruction, not a task at a point in a course, so all/general.

units.why: Principle 2 says the use of AI "should aim to advance the university's instructional mission", a framing principle for the whole guideline, so P56.
units.anchor: should aim to advance the university’s instructional mission
units.resolution_why: Only A found it. Principle 2 says AI use 'should aim to advance the university's instructional mission', a framing principle in the same framework; real policy statement, P56, kept.

units.why: Principle 3 states "Anything that is uploaded to a publicly available AI tool effectively enters the public domain", a privacy fact motivating data protection, so P50 as informs.
units.anchor: Anything that is uploaded to a publicly available AI tool effectively enters the public domain

units.why: "Generative AI tools which have not passed a campus security review may be used with public data only" limits unvetted tools to public data, so P50 (vetted tools, protect data); restrictive in effect.
units.anchor: may be used with public data only
units.fit_note: Also functions as a campus security review requirement (P65) for any tool used with non-public data.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase general, B during-work. The rule limits what data may go into unvetted tools when they are used, so during-work.

units.why: "UCR provides access to secure tools including Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot" names the institution-licensed tools for non-public data, so P92 rather than P17 because it is institution-wide.
units.anchor: UCR provides access to secure tools including Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B permit. The sentence names available tools and does not itself permit anything, so neutral.

units.why: Principle 4 gives "the Instructor of Record ... broad latitude to determine whether and how generative AI may be used", so the rule is set per instructor, P04.
units.anchor: Instructor of Record has broad latitude to determine whether and how generative AI

units.why: The latitude holds "provided this use is consistent with applicable policies and rules governing data security and instruction at UCR", so instructor choices must follow existing university policy, P77.
units.anchor: provided this use is consistent with applicable policies and rules governing data security
units.resolution_why: A coded neutral, B restrict. The condition ties instructor choices to existing policy; it adds no new limit on AI, so neutral.

units.why: Principle 5 says "Anyone using generative AI for any purpose is accountable for the consequences of their use", which holds users responsible for what they produce with AI, P29.
units.anchor: Anyone using generative AI for any purpose is accountable for the consequences of their use
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B require. 'accountable for the consequences' states responsibility without requiring or banning AI use, so neutral.
units.fit_note: Accountability for consequences of any AI use by anyone, not only ownership of submitted student work.

units.why: "Not all generative AI responses are accurate" states that output can be wrong, P31 as informs.
units.anchor: Not all generative AI responses are accurate
units.fit_note: States that output can be inaccurate but does not explicitly instruct users to verify it.

units.why: "some may violate intellectual property rights" names an IP risk of AI output, P52 as informs.
units.anchor: some may violate intellectual property rights

units.why: "Responses also may perpetuate biases inherent in model design and/or training datasets" names bias as a concern, P53.
units.anchor: may perpetuate biases inherent in model design and/or training datasets

units.why: Accountability "includes ... violations of academic integrity policies, other institutional policies and rules, and applicable laws", tying AI use to existing policies and law, P77.
units.anchor: violations of academic integrity policies, other institutional policies and rules, and applicable laws
units.resolution_why: A coded general, B when-misuse. The sentence defines the scope of accountability ('applies to all aspects of teaching and learning'); it states no sanction step, so general.

units.why: Principle 6 calls AI "a potentially useful and powerful information source and thought partner which can enhance productivity and learning", a benefit statement, P87.
units.anchor: useful and powerful information source and thought partner which can enhance productivity and learning
units.resolution_why: Only A found it. Principle 6 calls AI 'a potentially useful and powerful information source and thought partner which can enhance productivity and learning', a benefit statement (P87). Real statement, kept.

units.why: Principle 6 says anyone using AI "must conform with prevailing ethical scholarship practices, rules related to plagiarism", i.e. AI use falls under existing plagiarism and scholarship rules, closest to P45.
units.anchor: must conform with prevailing ethical scholarship practices, rules related to plagiarism
units.fit_note: The text applies scholarship and plagiarism rules to AI use rather than comparing AI to a human collaborator; it also mentions representing work as one's own (P29). (Coder B: Applies existing plagiarism and scholarship rules to AI use but does not compare AI to a human collaborator and does not explicitly require disclosure.)
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance permit, B restrict. The passage applies existing plagiarism and scholarship rules to AI without allowing or limiting use, so neutral.

units.why: Principle 6 requires "standards for representing intellectual products as one's own work" to be met, so submitted work must be presented as the student's own, P29.
units.anchor: standards for representing intellectual products as one’s own work
units.resolution_why: Only A found it. 'standards for representing intellectual products as one's own work' is a separate clause from the plagiarism-rules clause (B merged them into one P45 unit). It states a distinct ownership requirement, P29, kept.

units.why: The instructor practice "Adhering to AI security and privacy practices is vital to protecting UCR's intellectual property and individual user data" tells instructors to protect data, P50.
units.anchor: Adhering to AI security and privacy practices is vital to protecting UCR’s intellectual property

units.why: "Explore the capabilities of generative AI by logging into your UCR account and experimenting with tools such as Google Gemini" encourages instructors to learn the tools before setting policy, P63.
units.anchor: Explore the capabilities of generative AI by logging into your UCR account

units.why: "UCR has established contractual agreements with Google for its AI tools, which offer enhanced security and privacy" says which tools are institution-approved and why, P92.
units.anchor: UCR has established contractual agreements with Google for its AI tools
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all, B instructor. The contract fact is institution-wide information, although it sits in a list of instructor practices; all.

units.why: The practice lists how AI "can draft or revise sections of your syllabus, create lesson plans, summarize readings" and draft announcements, describing instructor uses of AI in teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: It can draft or revise sections of your syllabus, create lesson plans, summarize readings
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance permit, B encourage. 'It can draft or revise sections of your syllabus ...' lists what instructors may do with AI; it does not urge use, so permit.

units.why: "analyze spreadsheet data to identify trends in student performance, and provide personalized feedback" are further instructor uses of AI in course operations, P59.
units.anchor: analyze spreadsheet data to identify trends in student performance, and provide personalized feedback
units.resolution_why: A coded during-work, B before-course. Data analysis and personalized feedback occur while the course runs, so during-work.

units.why: "Consider how students can utilize generative AI, consistent with your course standards" leaves student uses to the instructor's course standards, P04.
units.anchor: Consider how students can utilize generative AI, consistent with your course standards
units.resolution_why: A coded encourage, B permit. 'Consider how students can utilize generative AI, consistent with your course standards' leaves student use to the course; it does not push use, so permit.

units.why: AI "can help students brainstorm topics for a writing assignment" names brainstorming as a student use, P15.
units.anchor: help students brainstorm topics for a writing assignment
units.resolution_why: A coded actor student, B instructor. The sentence sits in practices addressed to instructors ('Consider how students can utilize...'), so instructor. unit_stance permit (B) not encourage (A): it lists uses instructors may allow.

units.why: AI can "summarize research articles or class notes ... and generate practice problems including for Canvas quizzes" lists study and practice uses, P14.
units.anchor: summarize research articles or class notes, create presentation outlines, and generate practice problems
units.resolution_why: A coded actor student, B instructor. Same sentence and addressee as the brainstorming unit, so instructor; unit_stance permit.

units.why: "Consider implementing authentic assessment methods in your course" recommends changing assessment design in light of AI, P35.
units.anchor: Consider implementing authentic assessment methods in your course
units.fit_note: Suggests authentic methods (also naming oral exams, P34) that include the use of generative AI in the real world.

units.why: "You may need to change the outcomes you are assessing and/or the conditions under which the assessment takes place" advises redesigning traditional assessments for AI, P35.
units.anchor: change the outcomes you are assessing and/or the conditions under which the assessment takes place

units.why: The list of authentic methods includes "oral exams and presentations", which check understanding by having students explain their work, P34.
units.anchor: oral exams and presentations
units.fit_note: Offered as one of several authentic assessment examples, not as a check on suspected AI use.
units.resolution_why: Only A found it. 'oral exams and presentations' is named as an example of an authentic assessment method; B mentioned it only in a fit note. It is a distinct listed practice, P34 with a fit note, kept.

units.why: "XCITE offers resources and workshops to help you explore the possibilities" provides faculty support for learning AI, P63.
units.anchor: XCITE offers resources and workshops to help you explore the possibilities
units.resolution_why: A coded neutral, B encourage. The sentence only informs that XCITE offers workshops, so neutral.

units.why: "consider how you can achieve some degree of alignment of your course standards with those of your immediate colleagues" asks instructors to align course AI standards for department consistency; no type covers aligning standards across colleagues, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: achieve some degree of alignment of your course standards with those of your immediate colleagues
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should align their course AI standards with those of colleagues so students get department-level consistency.

units.why: "Establish clear expectations in your syllabus" tells instructors to put AI expectations in the syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: Establish clear expectations in your syllabus
units.resolution_why: A coded neutral, B require. The practice sets no AI rule itself; it tells instructors to state expectations, so neutral.

units.why: The same sentence adds "including how students should cite and document the use of generative AI in their work", a disclosure expectation to be set by instructors; P24 fits since it concerns citing and documenting AI use.
units.anchor: how students should cite and document the use of generative AI in their work
units.fit_note: The text tells instructors to specify citation expectations; it does not itself require students to disclose. (Coder B: Instructors are told to specify how students cite; the document does not itself require disclosure.)
units.resolution_why: A coded permit, B require. The sentence tells instructors to specify citation expectations; it does not itself permit or require AI use or disclosure, so neutral.

units.why: "XCITE has developed some suggested syllabus language which you can modify" offers syllabus templates as support for instructors, P63.
units.anchor: XCITE has developed some suggested syllabus language which you can modify
units.resolution_why: Only A found it. 'XCITE has developed some suggested syllabus language which you can modify' offers syllabus templates to instructors; real support statement, P63, kept.

units.why: "Also establish clear expectations for each assessment" asks instructors to state AI expectations per assessment, P09.
units.anchor: establish clear expectations for each assessment to help avoid potential problems related to academic integrity
units.resolution_why: A coded neutral, B require. Same reasoning: instructors are asked to state expectations; no stance on AI, so neutral.

units.why: "If you suspect academic misconduct, follow the standard campus procedures" points to the normal integrity process, P81.
units.anchor: If you suspect academic misconduct, follow the standard campus procedures
units.resolution_why: A coded should, B must. The passage is a 'suggested practice' under the heading 'Suggested Practices for Instructors', so should.

units.why: "automated AI detection tools can be inaccurate and prone to bias" tells instructors detectors are unreliable, P39.
units.anchor: automated AI detection tools can be inaccurate and prone to bias
units.resolution_why: A coded informs, B should-not. 'keep in mind that automated AI detection tools can be inaccurate' is a caution that states a fact; it does not forbid detectors, so informs.
units.fit_note: Cautions instructors that detectors are inaccurate; it does not say they must not be used.

units.why: "Share your own ideas about generative AI with your students, including how you are using it in your research and teaching" asks instructors to disclose their own AI use, P47.
units.anchor: including how you are using it in your research and teaching
units.fit_note: Also invites sharing views about AI generally, not only disclosure of the instructor's own use.

units.why: "Remind students that over-reliance on generative AI can undermine their education ... and likelihood of success on in-class assessments and in job interviews" gives a learning reason (P41) that also warns about exposure on assessments (P43); P41 chosen as the main point is undermined education.
units.anchor: over-reliance on generative AI can undermine their education
units.fit_note: Also warns that over-reliance hurts success on in-class assessments and in job interviews (P43 and P94 elements). (Coder B: Warns that over-reliance undermines education and later performance in exams and interviews; does not use the idea of a false sense of mastery.)
units.resolution_why: A coded P41, B P43. The passage says over-reliance 'can undermine their education, opportunities for intellectual growth', a limit-AI-because-it-skips-learning reason (P41). It does not describe a false sense of mastery (P43), though it mentions in-class assessments and interviews.

units.why: "contact the library at libteaching@ucr.edu" for "resources for students on ethical and responsible AI use" points instructors to student AI-literacy resources, P70.
units.anchor: resources for students on ethical and responsible AI use in their academic, research
units.fit_note: Directs instructors to library resources for students; not a mandated training.
units.resolution_why: A coded P70/before-course/informs, B P72/course-start/may. The sentence points instructors to library 'resources for students on ethical and responsible AI use', i.e. AI-literacy resources, P70; instructor-directed so before-course; informs because it names a resource and permits nothing.

documents.unit: Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs (student mailing list)
documents.title: [Students] Update on Artificial Intelligence Use
documents.summary: A 2023 Vice Chancellor message to students advising them to check with professors before using generative AI and to keep AI as help rather than a replacement for their own work. It adds tips on citing, privacy, and the consequences of plagiarism, and lists support offices.
documents.stance_why: The message sets no blanket rule and says "We encourage you to discuss with your professors for specific policies or expectations before engaging in the use of Generative AI" and "Follow the guidance of your professors", so the decision rests with instructors, though it advises against generating whole deliverables. Coder B reached the same stance.

units.why: "We encourage you to discuss with your professors for specific policies or expectations before engaging in the use of Generative AI" tells students to ask before using AI, P10.
units.anchor: discuss with your professors for specific policies or expectations before engaging
units.resolution_why: A coded before-course, B course-start. Students are told to learn the instructor's expectations before using AI; that is the expectations-communication phase, course-start.

units.why: "Follow the guidance of your professors for specific policies or expectations" makes students responsible for following each professor's AI rules, P78.
units.anchor: Follow the guidance of your professors for specific policies or expectations
units.resolution_why: A coded should, B must; A unit_stance neutral, B restrict. 'Follow the guidance of your professors' is an imperative with no hedge, so must; it adds no AI limit itself, so neutral. Coded once though repeated in two bullets.

units.why: "Using AI tools should assist or enhance, not replace, your original work" keeps the student as primary author, P32.
units.anchor: Using AI tools should assist or enhance, not replace, your original work

units.why: "the essence of academic work lies in original thought, critical analysis, and academic integrity" gives the reason for limiting AI as protecting the purpose of academic work, P95.
units.anchor: the essence of academic work lies in original thought, critical analysis, and academic integrity
units.fit_note: Mixes skill (original thought, critical analysis) with integrity; integrity chosen because the message pairs it with honesty.
units.resolution_why: Only A found it. 'the essence of academic work lies in original thought, critical analysis, and academic integrity' is the stated reason for limiting AI; real rationale, P95, kept.

units.why: "AI can produce responses that are not always accurate" is a warning that output can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: AI can produce responses that are not always accurate

units.why: AI responses "may violate intellectual property rights", an IP warning, P52.
units.anchor: may violate intellectual property rights
units.resolution_why: Only A found it. AI responses 'may violate intellectual property rights' is a separate IP warning; B folded it into the accuracy unit's topics. Distinct statement, P52, kept.

units.why: AI tools "may perpetuate biases inherent in their design and/or training datasets" names bias, P53.
units.anchor: may perpetuate biases inherent in their design and/or training datasets

units.why: "UCR has invested in several resources that can be used to bolster student research, learning, and academic projects" lists ARC, Conduct, Writing and Reading Support and the Library as human support, P72.
units.anchor: UCR has invested in several resources that can be used to bolster student research, learning

units.why: "AI can assist with data analysis" names a permitted use, P89.
units.anchor: AI can assist with data analysis

units.why: AI can "generate ideas, or help structure your thoughts", a brainstorming use, P15.
units.anchor: generate ideas, or help structure your thoughts

units.why: "you should not use it to generate essays, assignments, or other deliverables in their entirety" bars having AI produce the whole submission, P19.
units.anchor: you should not use it to generate essays, assignments, or other deliverables in their entirety
units.fit_note: Bans only generating whole deliverables; partial AI help is left open.

units.why: "Your work should reflect your understanding, thoughts, and efforts" asks that submitted work show the student's own understanding, P29.
units.anchor: Your work should reflect your understanding, thoughts, and efforts
units.resolution_why: A coded neutral, B restrict. 'Your work should reflect your understanding' says what the work should show without limiting AI by itself, so neutral.

units.why: "If you use AI-generated content or data ... ensure that you cite it properly" requires citing AI use, P24.
units.anchor: ensure that you cite it properly

units.why: AI tools "may not provide you with the citations from where they are generating their responses, making it extremely difficult to verify the quality of the information" warns output is hard to verify, P31.
units.anchor: making it extremely difficult to verify the quality of the information in their responses
units.resolution_why: A coded general, B during-work. A statement that tools give no citations and output is hard to verify is a fact, so general.
units.fit_note: Explains why verification is hard but does not explicitly tell students to verify.

units.why: "Always ensure that the software or platform you're using is from a reputable source and has adequate security measures" tells students to prefer vetted tools, P50.
units.anchor: Always ensure that the software or platform
units.resolution_why: A coded must/restrict, B should/neutral. 'Always ensure ...' is a tip in a list of 'a few tips', not a requirement, so should; it advises care and does not limit AI, so neutral.

units.why: "Avoid sharing personal or sensitive information" protects personal data when using AI, P50.
units.anchor: Avoid sharing personal or sensitive information

units.why: "be wary of freely available online AI tools that may not have clearly stated privacy policies" cautions about unvetted tools, P50.
units.anchor: be wary of freely available online AI tools
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose P50/should. B's anchor was copied from a different sentence (the plagiarism sentence), so A's anchor, which is in the source, is used.

units.why: "individual responsibility plays a significant role in maintaining this safety net" places part of data protection on the student, P50.
units.anchor: individual responsibility plays a significant role in maintaining this safety net
units.resolution_why: Only A found it. 'individual responsibility plays a significant role in maintaining this safety net' places part of data protection on the student; real statement, P50, kept.

units.why: "plagiarizing AI-generated content, will result in serious consequences" classes improper AI use as a breach of academic integrity, P36.
units.anchor: Breaching academic integrity, which includes plagiarizing AI-generated content, will result in serious consequences

units.why: Consequences "may range from receiving a failing grade for the assignment to more severe academic penalties" states penalties in advance, P37.
units.anchor: receiving a failing grade for the assignment to more severe academic penalties
units.resolution_why: A coded prohibit, B neutral. The sentence states penalties in advance without stating a stance on AI, so neutral.

units.why: "honesty and integrity are fundamental educational and community values" gives the integrity-culture reason for the rules, P95.
units.anchor: honesty and integrity are fundamental educational and community values

units.why: "develop a clear understanding of the University's policies ... to represent yourself truthfully, to claim only work that is your own" makes students responsible for submitting their own work, P29.
units.anchor: to claim only work that is your own
units.resolution_why: A coded general/neutral, B during-work/restrict. The sentence is a closing reminder to understand integrity policies, not a rule at a point in the work, so general; it limits no AI use, so neutral.

units.why: "Our faculty, staff, and academic advisors are always here to guide you and answer any queries you may have regarding the appropriate use of AI" points students to human help, P72.
units.anchor: Our faculty, staff, and academic advisors are always here to guide you

notes: Course layer was deferred in collection. The 2023-08 faculty guidelines were not collected. One UNCOVERED unit (aligning course AI standards with colleagues). Reconciled from coders A and B. Coder B. Course layer deferred; no school or computing policy found. The students email repeats 'Follow the guidance of your professors' in two bullets; coded once.
